title: Bournemouth agree £26m fee for Benfica defender Silva
description: Bournemouth agree a deal worth up to almost £26m for Benfica centre-back Antonio Silva.
fullText:
Bournemouth have agreed a deal worth up to almost £26m for Benfica centre-back Antonio Silva.

The Portugal international, 22, is travelling for a medical after the two clubs reached an agreement worth an initial £21.4m, plus a further £4.3m in add-ons.

It is a key signing for the Cherries, who identified replacing Marcos Senesi, following his free-transfer move to Tottenham earlier this month, as a priority.

Club sources say a move for Silva has required patience, with an agreement only reached after Benfica's Europa League qualifying-round victory over Swiss side St Gallen on Thursday.

Silva has been a regular for Benfica since breaking into the first team in 2022 and has featured in the Champions League, Europa League and Club World Cup.

He has 20 caps and was in Portugal's squads for the 2022 World Cup and Euro 2024 but was not selected by Roberto Martinez for this summer's tournament.

Silva is expected to become Bournemouth's second signing of the summer after the arrival of striker Alvaro Rodriguez from Elche in a deal worth up to £25.7m.

Bournemouth, who have a new manager in Marco Rose, are aiming for a summer of stability after selling more than £200m worth of players last year.

They are determined to resist offers for three of their key players - Alex Scott, Rayan and Junior Kroupi.

Kroupi is out for three to four months, having suffered an injury in pre-season training.

title: 'Naturally it's going to' - Palmer says England snub gives extra motivation
description: Chelsea forward Cole Palmer says being told he was "essentially not good enough" to make England's World Cup squad will serve as extra motivation this season.  The 24-year-old was controversially left out of Thomas Tuchel's squad, with England finishing third.  Palmer competed at the Club World Cup, the European Championship and the European Under-21 Championship before enjoying his first summer holiday as a professional footballer this time around.
fullText:
Chelsea forward Cole Palmer says being told he was "essentially not good enough" to make England's World Cup squad will serve as extra motivation this season.

The 24-year-old was controversially left out of Thomas Tuchel's squad, with England finishing third.

Palmer competed at the Club World Cup, the European Championship and the European Under-21 Championship before enjoying his first summer holiday as a professional footballer this time around.

He said he went to Marbella with his family but found the experience "strange" at first, admitting he "got bored after six weeks" and was eager to return.

"I never thought I'd think that," he added. "I was checking when I was back in."

Asked whether missing the World Cup would provide extra motivation, Palmer said: "Yes, naturally it's going to. It's like anything. If someone tells you you're essentially not good enough to get in the squad, then you're going to think, 'All right then, I'm going to try to go that extra bit harder'."

The playmaker also revealed it was "nice" when new Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso sent him a message soon after learning he had missed out on England selection.

He also spoke about his groin injury last season, which impacted his form, saying he played on it when he "probably shouldn't have done".

Palmer, who admitted he sought specialist advice over whether surgery was needed to address the recurring problem, added: "I feel good now. The seven weeks obviously helped. I'm ready to go again."

title: AC Milan and Italy great Baresi dies aged 66
description: AC Milan and Italy great Franco Baresi has died at the age of 66, the Italian club announces.
fullText:
Franco Baresi has died at the age of 66, with AC Milan saying their former captain's "example and integrity will be forever etched into the club's DNA".

Baresi spent his entire 20-year playing career with the club from 1977 until he retired in 1997, winning six Serie A titles and three European Cups/Champions Leagues.

Regarded as one of the greatest defenders to play the game, Baresi captained Milan for 15 seasons, making 719 appearances and scoring 33 goals.

He was capped 81 times by Italy and was part of the squad which won the 1982 World Cup. He played and was captain in the 1994 final, which Italy lost to Brazil.

In 2020, Baresi became honorary vice-president of AC Milan, with the club retiring his number six shirt four years later.

Baresi formed part of one of European football's most celebrated defences alongside Paolo Maldini, Alessandro Costacurta and Mauro Tassotti.

He also lifted four Supercoppa Italianas, two European Super Cups and the Intercontinental Cup twice.

In the 1994 World Cup, he returned from a knee injury to play in the final and largely nullified the threat of Brazil's Romario and Bebeto in a 0-0 draw.

It was the first World Cup final to be decided by a shootout and Baresi missed the first penalty, with Brazil eventually winning it 3-2.

Baresi had surgery in August 2025 to remove a lung nodule, and his last public appearance was at the San Siro Stadium for the Winter Olympics opening ceremony in February.

In a statement on X, AC Milan wrote: "Milan is in tears following the passing of Franco Baresi. His example and integrity will be forever etched into the club's DNA, just as his iconic number 6 shirt is."

In a further post on the club's website, they added: "Announcing the loss of someone who embodied the heart and soul of AC Milan is incredibly difficult. But everyone at the club and all the Milanisti must live up to Franco Baresi's memory.

"In memory of Franco, we stand united, knowing he'll guide and push us throughout our Rossoneri journey. Forever. Because Baresi is forever."

title: AC Milan and Italy great Franco Baresi dies aged 66
description: Former AC Milan and Italy defender Franco Baresi has died aged 66, Milan have said. The former Milan captain is widely regarded as one of the finest defenders in football history and spent his entire career with the club, playing 719 times in 20 seasons as a professional.
fullText:
Former AC Milan and Italy defender Franco Baresi has died aged 66, Milan have said.

The former Milan captain is widely regarded as one of the finest defenders in football history and spent his entire career with the club, playing 719 times in 20 seasons as a professional.

During that time Baresi won six Serie A crowns, with his first Scudetto coming as a teenager during the 1978-79 campaign and he lifted five further titles in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

The defender also won three European Cups, two Intercontinental Cups and four Italian Supercups during his career and his contributions to Milan saw the club retire the number six jersey.

On the international stage, Baresi was part of the Italy squad which won the World Cup in 1982, as well as featuring in the 1994 World Cup, which ended in a penalty shootout defeat to Brazil in the final.

A post on the official Milan X account said: “The entire history of AC Milan is in tears following the passing of Franco Baresi.

“His example and integrity will be forever etched into the club’s DNA, just as his iconic number 6 shirt is.

“The condolences AC Milan extends to Franco Baresi’s family at such a difficult time are shared by every Rossonero, who feels this loss as their own.”

In a further statement on the club website, Milan added: “Announcing the loss of someone who embodied the heart and soul of AC Milan, is incredibly difficult.

“But everyone at the club and all the Milanisti must live up to Franco Baresi’s memory. We must be strong and gather every bit of energy, even at this saddest of times.

“We lost Franco only a few months after his last public appearance in a packed San Siro, at the Milan Winter Olympics opening ceremony, an event on the world stage he helped make unforgettable.

“In memory of Franco, we stand united, knowing he’ll guide and push us throughout our Rossoneri journey. Forever. Because Baresi is forever.”

title: USA250: 10 greatest college athletes from Virginia ranked
description: Virginia and Virginia Tech make up most of the 10 greatest college athletes in the history of the commonwealth - but not all the spots on our list.
fullText:
The Commonwealth of Virginia might be best known in college athletics for its major schools — Virginia and Virginia Tech.

However, the two Atlantic Coast Conference members don't have a monopoly on the best players to have participated in the state.

That's because there are 14 other Division I institutions that have their own standouts worthy of consideration for our list of best athletes from Virginia colleges. Old Dominion had two selections, and there were other contenders from Liberty, James Madison and Richmond who narrowly missed out.

But our list can only include 10, so here's the best of the bunch:

One of the dominant defensive linemen of his generation, Smith had 46 sacks in his career with the Hokies. The impressive total includes 22, which led the country in his junior season. As a senior, Smith was a consensus All-American and won the Outland Trophy before becoming the No. 1 overall pick in the 1985 NFL draft.

Vick redshirted his first season before becoming one of the most exciting players in the country in his two playing campaigns with the Hokies. The left-handed quarterback led Tech to an unbeaten regular season and appearance in the Bowl Championship Series title game in 1999 while finishing third in the Heisman Trophy race. She led the Monarchs to consecutive AIAW national championships in 1979 and 1980 and was a two-time winner of the Wade Trophy, given to the top player in the country. Her 961 assists still stand as the top mark in school history.

Small in size, Staley produced one of the great careers in women's college basketball. She led the Cavaliers to three consecutive Final Four appearances and was the tournament's most outstanding player when Virginia lost to Tennessee in the 1991 title game. She was a national champion in 25 events with nine individual titles, including four consecutive victories in 100-meter freestyle. Walsh won the Honda Award as the top women's collegiate athlete in all sports during the 2024-25 academic year.

No college baseball pitcher from the commonwealth accumulated more strikeouts than Verlander, who posted 427 in his 335 2/3 innings across three seasons with the Monarchs. A freshman All-American, he would go on to be a dominant force as a sophomore and junior, becoming a finalist for the Roger Clemons National pitcher of the Year award and eventually the No. 2 overall pick in the 2004 MLB draft.

At a school with a rich men's lacrosse history, Shellenberger holds the school record for points (323) and the ACC record for assists (192). description: PCB is deciding the PSL 2027 (PSL 12) window to avoid an IPL clash.

PCB debates PSL 2027 window: clash with IPL or February-March return.

Pakistan's cricket board finds itself at a crossroads over when to stage the next edition of Pakistan Super League (PSL), and it still remains undecided on whether the competition should run alongside the Indian Premier League or shift back to its old February-March home.

According to Mian Ahmad, PCB representatives and franchise owners debated two possible scheduling slots for PSL 2027 during a recent meeting in Lahore, with the cricket committee expected to finalise things after more deliberation.

Both the 2025 and 2026 editions of the league were held during the April-May period, which put them in direct competition with the IPL after that tournament moved off its usual February-March calendar.

If PSL return to the earlier window, it would sidestep any overlap with the IPL, making it far more likely that PSL franchises could secure their top overseas recruits without scheduling conflicts. Officials pointed to additional perks too, including more favourable weather and stronger commercial prospects for sponsors during that period.

That said, there are complications to consider. An earlier slot risks bumping into other international franchise leagues around the world, and it would also fall during the holy month of Ramadan, which could throw up its own set of logistical hurdles.

However, hosting matches in April-May through Pakistan's peak summer heat isn't ideal, and the timing would also clash with school exam season. The cricket committee is set to keep talking before settling on a final recommendation.

Beyond the scheduling question, the same meeting also touched on a proposal to add a Super Six stage to the tournament format, though sources indicated that plan hinges on sorting out a financial dispute involving one of the league's commercial partners first.

Officials reportedly raised concerns about unpaid dues owed by a major stakeholder, and when that company's representative addressed the room, PCB officials pushed back firmly, reminding them of their contractual commitments and warning that continued delays wouldn't be tolerated.

Franchise owners backed a hardline approach, and argued that teams themselves face penalties for late payments and that commercial partners should be held to the same standard. Everyone present agreed the matter needed resolving by Monday, following a run of board meetings held over the weekend.

A separate idea was floated at the meeting which would let the PCB recover unpaid commercial dues by deducting them from a franchise fee. This is applicable in cases where a company both owns a team and holds a separate commercial deal with the league.

Scheduling clashes with the IPL have quietly hurt the PSL's ability to attract marquee overseas talent for two years running, and that's not a small issue for a league trying to build its global reputation.

Cooler weather and better sponsor engagement are nice bonuses, but the core problem remains simple: fans want to watch the best players, and franchises want them too.

A February-March return, even with the Ramadan complication, seems like the more sensible long-term move if the PCB genuinely wants the PSL to compete with the world's biggest T20 leagues rather than just fill dates on a calendar.

title: Can boxing ‘addiction’ ever be cured? Pain of retiring explored in new Sky documentary
description: IN FOCUS: Alex Pattle dives into the Sky Sports film ‘The Final Round’ and speaks to champion turned pundit Johnny Nelson, a key voice in the documentary
fullText:
Sky Sports’s new documentary is stacked with sobering soundbites. In one scene, boxing coach Joe Gallagher recalls hearing a mother ask her son: “Are all the lows worth that one high?” The answer, of course, was “yes”. As Gallagher puts it: “Everyone wants their own Rocky story.”

But as Sky explores, that doesn’t always mean a rousing underdog story. Rocky’s sequels showed Sylvester Stallone’s character struggling with retirement, and this is the premise of The Final Round.

Releasing on Friday, the film features interviews with former world champions like Johnny Nelson and Josh Warrington, while Gallagher and Dominic Ingle are among the coaches to speak, promoter Eddie Hearn features, and commentator Andy Clarke weaves together themes of “addiction”, sacrifice, and ego.

The documentary even includes one of the final interviews with the late, great Ricky Hatton, whose internal fights after retiring matched any that he had in the ring.

Many boxers tell themselves, “‘I’ve got one more good fight in me,’” Hatton says. “Nine times out of 10, you haven’t. That was the case with me.”

Indeed, in 2022, a 42-year-old Hatton boxed Marco Antonio Barrera in an exhibition, and he was even due for another before his untimely death last September.

“Ego never leaves a fighter, and that’s the problem,” Nelson says. It outlasts the “fire”, he adds, shrewdly touching on an unfair fight between the two emotions.

Yet it’s not just about fire and ego; a question of identity arises, as does a fear of life post-boxing. Retirement is “frightening”, says heavyweight veteran Dave Allen, who reversed his own exit from the sport. “Apart from ‘Dad’, I’m just a boxer. I’m not even David, the normal human being.”

Warrington, whose boxing future is up in the air at the time of writing, explains: “I wake up on fight day and it’s like everything’s brighter, everything smells better, I’m more alert... that’s an unreal feeling.” And then the kicker: “Once that stops, you’ll never feel it again.”

Does this explain Tyson Fury’s five false retirements? Perhaps. They get their own spotlight in the documentary, as do comebacks that occur decades after retirement: for example, a 58-year-old Mike Tyson facing a 27-year-old YouTuber, Jake Paul, in 2024.

The film touches on how boxers don’t just miss the buzz of fight night, but also the camaraderie of their gyms, while the financial turmoil that has afflicted many fighters gets significant screen time.

Most boxers need a second job, and promoter and manager Steve Wood explains: “Ninety per cent of the fighters I look after are not earning enough to pay tax. I’ve had a couple of world champions; they’re the only two likely to be able to retire comfortably.”

In an interview with The Independent, Nelson touches on all of these topics, as well as his plans to create a proper pension scheme for boxers – something his own promoter, Eddie’s father Barry Hearn, attempted unsuccessfully.

Barry tried putting a small percentage of boxers’ purses towards a pension, but fighters’ distrust and/or short-term thinking thwarted the plan. Nelson, who toyed with his own comeback nine years after retiring, reflects on receiving a £97,000 pension from Hearn several years ago, inspiring the 59-year-old.

Nelson wants to create a scheme that would pay £2,000 into a pension for each boxer every year, as long as the fighter competes two to three times annually and puts 5 per cent of their purse into the same pension – with the money coming from a combination of TV companies, government grants, and private sponsorship. Nelson has spoken to the British Boxing Board of Control, figures in parliament, Scottish Widows, and potential financiers while trying to get the scheme off the ground.

“If I was a parent and my son wanted to box, I wouldn’t want him to box for a career, because they’ve got nothing to show for it,” Nelson says. “There’s no aftercare. Everybody’s running for the trees, nobody wants to take responsibility for the fighters creating the entertainment.

“The amount of household names I could tell you that are absolutely on their ass, they’ve got nothing, and that financial pressure on top of the other effects of boxing has accumulated over the years. How can your mental health be stable? How can it be?”

In general, Nelson articulates the existence of a boxer with ease.

“That animalistic instinct we have, there’s nothing you can adapt it to in everyday life – not an office or anything like that, because it’s barbaric,” he says. “It’s a very lonely existence. Your wife, brother, mother, sister don’t get it. The aches and pains are lonely, the thought processes are lonely.

“You do it first for the love of it, then money comes into it, then ups and downs, so we still do it – but resentfully. You’ve not got time to have a full-time job, so [you may think]: ‘People see me on a dizzy high, and then I’ve got to go and work on a building site. God, I've got to deal with the shame of that.’

“You’re resentful of how human nature can change: when you retire, people no longer look up to you as an amazing fighter. ‘He’s overweight, he’s not who he was.’ They talk to you like they talk to anybody, whereas when you’re a fighter, they talk to you with respect.”

Nelson is now one of the most thoughtful and respected pundits in boxing, but he could not have foreseen this future while immersed in his past.

“I thought boxing was the only option I had,” he reflects. “I left school with the reading and writing ability of a 10-year-old. I wasn’t thick – I just wasn’t academically astute – but I thought I was. I’d got nothing on paper to say, ‘Johnny is really good with people,’ so that wisdom doesn’t get you a job. What gets you a job is a diploma, work experience. So, panic set in. I could have easily ended up in prison.”

As The Final Round shows, boxing can be its own kind of prison, but a champion who escaped relatively early and safely was Anthony Crolla, who retired on a win just before turning 33.

“You can’t let boxing take more from you than you take from boxing,” he says astutely in the film. If only it were that simple.

title: The Premier League clubs fighting a World Cup hangover
description: Which Premier League clubs have carried the biggest World Cup workload?
fullText:
The Premier League season begins on 21 August - just 33 days after the World Cup final.

For some clubs, that leaves barely enough time to welcome players back from the mandatory three-week post-tournament break required under Fifa regulations, let alone integrate them into pre-season preparations.

Four Tottenham players were still involved on the final weekend of the tournament and may have little more than a week of training before the new campaign starts. Chelsea too were significantly affected.

And Manchester City and Arsenal have their own concerns after seeing more players than any other Premier League club reach the latter stages of the competition.

The World Cup may be over, but its impact on the Premier League is only just beginning.

Tottenham are among the clubs whose pre-season preparations have been most significantly impacted.

Cristian Romero and new signing Marcos Senesi reached the final with Argentina, while Pedro Porro helped Spain lift the trophy. Djed Spence remained with England until the third-place play-off on 18 July.

Assuming players take the minimum three weeks off under Fifa guidelines, Romero, Senesi and Porro would not return until 9 August, while Spence's earliest return date would be 8 August.

That leaves them with around two weeks to reintegrate before their Premier League season begins at Brentford on 22 August.

For managers, the challenge is not simply the absence itself. Players returning so late miss much of pre-season's tactical work, conditioning sessions and friendly matches, creating a difficult balancing act between preparation and recovery.

Manchester City and Arsenal, meanwhile, had the greatest concentration of players making deep runs into the competition.

City's World Cup contingent featured for several of the tournament's leading nations.

Rodri helped Spain win their second men's World Cup after playing 726 minutes, while Marc Guehi and Elliot Anderson helped England reach the final weekend.

Nico O'Reilly featured in England's semi-final run, while Erling Haaland and Jeremy Doku both reached the quarter-finals.

Arsenal's numbers were similarly striking.

Declan Rice and Bukayo Saka remained involved until England's 6-4 victory over France in the third-place play-off, while Martin Zubimendi and Mikel Merino reached the final with Spain.

William Saliba helped France reach the third-place play-off, although he was subsequently injured and did not feature again. Noni Madueke was part of England's run to the final weekend but did not play beyond the quarter-finals, while Martin Odegaard captained Norway to the quarter-finals.

The workload concerns are already being felt. City's Rodri recently had back surgery and is expected to miss a "short period" at the start of the season, while Saliba avoided surgery, but Arsenal have confirmed he will be sidelined for an "extended period" because of a back issue.

Even though neither setback can be attributed solely to the World Cup, both underline the physical demands being placed on players in an increasingly crowded football calendar.

Those clubs are likely to begin the campaign without having enjoyed a full pre-season with several key players.

The World Cup's biggest workload belonged to Aston Villa goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez, who played all 810 minutes of Argentina's run to the final.

Liverpool midfielder Alexis Mac Allister ranked second among Premier League players with 749 minutes, while Spain midfielder Rodri was third on 726.

Several players effectively completed the equivalent of eight full matches during the tournament.

Goalkeepers naturally face different physical demands from outfield players, but the figures underline the extent of Premier League involvement throughout the competition.

With the players entitled to a minimum three-week break under Fifa regulations, for those involved in the final on 19 July - including Rodri, Porro, Zubimendi, Mac Allister, Enzo Fernandez, Emiliano Martinez and Lisandro Martinez - the earliest return date is 9 August.

Players who featured in England's third-place play-off will return a day earlier.

That leaves clubs with roughly 12 days to reintegrate some of their most important players before competitive football begins.

The concerns extend beyond this summer's World Cup.

Many of football's leading players have now experienced three consecutive summers of major tournaments, following Euro 2024 and Copa America, then last year's expanded Club World Cup and now the World Cup.

One of those players is Rodri, who warned in 2024 that footballers were "close" to striking because of workload concerns.

Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta and Chelsea boss Enzo Maresca have also voiced concerns about the demands being placed on elite players and the growing number of matches in the calendar.

The growing injury list during the World Cup provided another reminder of those concerns.

Aston Villa midfielder Amadou Onana suffered a serious knee injury while representing Belgium, while Manchester United and Uruguay defensive midfielder Manuel Ugarte saw his tournament cut short by injury. Reece James also had his minutes carefully managed by England as he continued his recovery from a hamstring problem.

For clubs such as Tottenham, Arsenal, Manchester City and Chelsea, the challenge is now immediate.

The World Cup has concluded. The countdown to the Premier League season is under way.

But for some players, recovery comes first, and the race to be ready for opening weekend has only just begun.

title: "A race of upgrades" - How development will decide the 2026 F1 title
description: The development race is starting to decide the F1 2026 pecking order and Stella reckons this'll continue until the end
fullText:
The 2026 Formula 1 season is shaping up how it was expected to be, with the development race deciding the pecking order as the campaign progresses. Although Mercedes started this regulation cycle in dominant form, winning the opening six grands prix from pole, it has ‘only’ won two of the last five with Ferrari and McLaren entering the fray.

Ferrari, in particular, has made headlines thanks to the raft of upgrades it brought in early 2026, drawing questions from Mercedes boss Toto Wolff about how this was possible under the cost cap.

The Scuderia nevertheless took much-needed wins in Barcelona and Silverstone, while last weekend in Hungary Lando Norris won by 15s from pole after his McLaren team updated five components on its MCL40: a modified rear wing endplate, new floor and floor board, revised front and rear corner furniture, plus an enlarged brake cooling outlet.

It was staggering how much the Woking outfit’s pace transcended at the Hungaroring - where it claimed a third consecutive victory and could have finished 1-2 had Oscar Piastri not retired with a gearbox fault late on - with its improved aerodynamic package working a treat at the tight and twisty circuit. To go from no man’s land in third to being in the mix amongst the top two showed how valuable an efficient development plan is this year, considering the freshness of the ruleset.

This is the biggest regulation overhaul in recent F1 history and just 11 rounds into the era, teams are still trying to learn their cars and understand which direction to take them. So, McLaren boss Andrea Stella expects this fight to continue and reckons it’ll decide who is the quickest come the season finale - currently scheduled to be Abu Dhabi on 4-6 December, but the ongoing Middle Eastern conflict puts that in doubt.

2026 season won't end in Las Vegas, F1 boss confirms

Stella said: “The improvement from a competitiveness point of view can be entirely ascribed to the upgrades that we took here. But at the same time, we were sort of thinking that this lap time step [would] not necessarily have been enough to be in pole position at the Hungaroring.

“Definitely we would not [have] thought that there would be enough to have such a strong pace in the race. Honestly, I still believe that if we want to be in a position to fight for victories consistently in the future, we need to keep our focus on delivering more upgrades.

“That is the plan, but we are not naive. We know that this will be the plan for all the teams. So I think like it's always been in this 2026 season, it's a matter of a race of upgrades. The good news is that McLaren is now back in this race of upgrades while fighting for the lead.

“But I expect that the car that will be the best car at the end of the season will keep adding tenths of a second in the next 11 [12 currently scheduled] races, probably as much as half a second. So, definitely a lot of work ahead of everyone, not only McLaren.”

Stella’s team knows better than any of the current crop how important upgrades can be.

Taking the last regulation cycle, for example, ground effect from 2022 to 2025, McLaren started it as a firm midfielder but then upgrades in 2023 eventually led to the team overtaking the previously dominant Red Bull to win the 2024 and 2025 titles.

As such, the Woking outfit has no plans to slow down and factored this into the budget cap, knowing “2026 would have been not much about the starting point, but more about the race to upgrade”. It is therefore expected to bring further updates at the next race in Zandvoort on 21-23 August, before finally fitting its Ferrari-style ‘Macarena Wing’ for the low-downforce Monza two weeks later.

But Stella is reluctant to confirm whether this’ll result in McLaren fighting Mercedes and the Scuderia consistently, because while the reigning champions might fit upgrades efficiently, so are the other teams - highlighted by Ferrari’s victories in 2026.

“There will be a few things coming for the next races,” said Stella. “This year, pretty much the top teams have always been successful in introducing upgrades to what I can see. I think this is because the rules are still relatively immature and the opportunities in terms of developing the car are almost low hanging fruit to cash in.

“So I don't think McLaren has any particular advantage in like, ‘oh everything we take is successful’. I think everyone is now doing a good job in terms of bringing successful upgrades. It will be more about how many upgrades the top teams will be in condition to deliver so far and for what's left of the season, because we are only midway in this season.”

title: Check out the social media trick the Pacers used to roll out uniform announcement
description: Prior to their uniform announcement Thursday, the first letter of their previous 17 tweets formed the phrase Pinstripes Are Back. Check it out
fullText:
The Pacers' social media team started leaving breadcrumbs a week ago leading to the announcement of their new pinstriped Statement uniforms. Just before the formal announcement, they pointed back at the trail.

The Pacers posted a photo graphic of the uniforms with tweets clamoring for a return of the pinstripes. The post read: "Please go back and read the first letter of our last 17 tweets," with two eye emojis.

Indeed, the first letter of that tweet and the previous 16 spelled out "PINSTRIPES ARE BACK."

The pattern was never obvious in large part because the letters were posted in reverse order chronologically so that scrolling through the timeline would spell out the words. So the last letter -- K -- was posted first on July 23 in a post about newly acquired Pacers forward Kelly Oubre Jr. highlighting a quote in a podcast from general manager Chad Buchanan. It wasn't until Wednesday that any of the posts even touched on the topic of uniforms as the social media team kept the bit going through tweets about Obi Toppin's charity golf outing, video of Tyrese Haliburton dunking during his Achilles tendon injury recovery, Toppin's serving as the pace car driver at the Brickyard 400 and the appearances of Jarace Walker and Braden Smith at basketball camps.

title: Mullins named manager at League Two Newport County
description: Hayden Mullins leaves his role as Fulham Under-21 boss to become the new head coach of League Two side Newport County.
fullText:
Newport County have appointed Fulham Under-21 boss Hayden Mullins as their new manager.

The Exiles have been without a permanent boss since the shock departure of Christian Fuchs in late June.

Following the exit of Fuchs - a 2015-16 Premier League title-winner with Leicester City - Newport appointed Chris Todd as their interim manager.

But the League Two club have now named ex-Crystal Palace, West Ham United and Portsmouth player Mullins as their new permanent boss.

Newport assistant manager Mark Smith has departed the club.

Todd, who has overseen Newport's pre-season friendlies against Bristol Manor Farm, Newport City, Gloucester City and Reading, is expected to remain at County.

Latest Newport County news, analysis and fan views

Listen to the latest Newport County news

Newport were four points adrift of safety in the fourth tier when Fuchs was named as Dave Hughes' successor in November last year.

The Austrian guided Newport to survival in League Two, but left the club on the eve of their return for pre-season ahead of the 2026-27 campaign.

The arrival of Mullins means it is the third successive summer that there has been a managerial change at Rodney Parade.

He is also the fourth permanent boss appointed by owner Huw Jenkins since his January 2024 takeover of the club, following Nelson Jardim, Hughes and Fuchs in the hot seat.

Former England Under-21 international Mullins - who also played for Reading, Birmingham City and Notts County - moved into coaching within Watford's youth system in 2016.

Having managed the Hornets' under-23s, he twice took temporary charge of Watford's senior team, following the exits of Quique Sánchez Flores and Nigel Pearson from Vicarage Road.

Mullins joined Colchester United as an assistant in 2020 and - following a stint as interim boss - took permanent charge of the U's in May 2021, but was sacked less than a year later.

He went on to have a brief stint in charge of the Turks and Caicos Islands national team in 2023 before joining Fulham as under-21 boss later that year.

In his first campaign in charge, Mullins led the young Cottagers to Premier League Cup glory with a 4-0 victory over Tottenham Hotspur Under-21s in the final.

Mullins will take charge of the first-team squad with immediate effect. His first match in the dugout will come on Saturday when County face Yeovil in pre-season.

Newport round off their summer schedule with a glamour meeting with Italian giants Roma at Rodney Parade on Tuesday, 4 August (19:00 BST).

They start their competitive schedule in the first round of the Carabao Cup at AFC Wimbledon on Saturday, 8 August (15:00 BST).

Newport then get their League Two campaign under way against Rochdale at Rodney Parade on Saturday, 15 August (12:30 BST).

title: Fifa says 'nobody selling football' as plan continues
description: Football's governing body Fifa plans to continue the consultation process after Uefa threatens to boycott World Cups.
fullText:
Fifa says that "nobody is selling football" as it vowed to continue with the controversial plan to sell stakes in its competitions to private investors.

Uefa - the body that governs European football - voted on Thursday to boycott World Cups if the plan proceeded.

Concacaf, which governs football in North and Central America and hosted this year's World Cup, said its 41 member associations also "rejected" the proposal made by Fifa president Gianni Infantino.

Fifa oversees world football and Infantino would need 106 of its 211 members to vote in favour for the proposal to go through. Uefa and Concacaf members combined make up 96 of those votes.

In a statement released on Friday, Fifa claimed the consultation process had been "disrupted by incorrect media reports".

"We respect the feedback and concern aired in public and reaffirm our commitment to an open and democratic consultation," the statement read.

"We will proceed with this consultation process to ensure that each MA (member association) has the ability to express its vote based on facts.

"Nobody is selling football. This is not something Fifa would ever entertain."

Is Infantino finished? Could Uefa boycott World Cup? What happens now?

Uefa to boycott World Cups if Fifa plans approved

Fifa offers $40m if nations back controversial plan

Fifa wants to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including its World Cups, and external investors will be able to buy stakes in it.

It said it would "invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).

In a 25-page document created by investment bank JP Morgan, it is made clear that Fifa's tournaments will expand to hit an estimated increased pay-out of 24m euros per member association in the 2035-2039 cycle.

It mentions "new business initiatives" and "attracting top talent with incentive-driven compensation".

The World Cup is described in it as the "most widely viewed" sporting event but Fifa, by contrast, is said to be "under-monetised".

There is no mention in the document of the women's game.

On Friday, Fifa said FFE had been proposed "to ensure all Fifa member associations have the opportunity to take meaningful ownership of the commercial opportunity of football in their respective countries".

"This does not come at the cost of either the spirit or the governance of Fifa or football itself," it added.

Infantino previously wrote to Fifa members saying they will receive $40m (£30m) if they back his controversial proposal. He set a deadline of 19 September for federations to accept his plans if they want to access an initial $20m (£15m).

However, Uefa has accused Fifa of using football "to enrich themselves and their friends".

If approval is granted, Fifa says Thrive Eternal is expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE.

Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner - the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.

Courting controversy and befriending Trump - the story of Fifa boss Infantino

Uefa and Concacaf have led the opposition to Infantino's plan.

"The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product," Uefa's statement on Thursday read.

"It is one of football's greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent.

"No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale.

"This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of Fifa's duty as the custodian of world football."

Concacaf said its members "expressed deep concerns about the lack of due process surrounding the proposal" and the "artificially short deadline imposed".

It also questioned the need for private investment after what Fifa claimed was the most profitable World Cup in history.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said that it is "deeply concerned that Fifa's unilateral actions appear to undermine the very foundations of continental football".

The AFC also said it was "unacceptable" that it had not been consulted before the proposal was publicly announced, nor provided with "detailed governance, financial or legal analysis".

The governing body overseeing football in South America, Conmebol, is yet to publicly comment on the proposals. The governing bodies in Africa (CAF) and Oceania (OFC) have said they will discuss Fifa's plan in August.

Chelsea manager and 2010 World Cup winner Xabi Alonso was asked about the situation during his side's pre-season tour of Australia.

"I think that football has to be for the people, not in private hands and I think that the way we love it is this way and we have seen a great World Cup and it's good to defend the interests of all the people," he said.

"Hopefully it won't happen and we will do it - we will keep the game as attractive and as authentic as we like it and that's why it creates these emotions, these passions."

It feels as though no-one who matters knows how this situation is going to play out just yet.

"Not sure the detail was considered when deciding the overall policy," was the response from a senior European football source when asked what this decision means for the U20 Women's World Cup, starting on 5 September, being hosted by Poland and featuring plenty of European nations.

Uefa's boycott threat will be activated if Infantino's funding deal is accepted.

Given 19 September is the deadline for countries to accept Fifa's deal and bank $20m (£15m) on 1 January, in theory, countries could be pulling out of that tournament in the middle of the quarter-finals and before the semis.

After that, the next senior matches in a Fifa competition are the Women's World Cup play-offs in October, which feature England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland among others.

Infantino became Fifa president in 2016 when he beat Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman al-Khalifa by 115 votes to 88. The Swiss is due to stand for a fourth term in March.

Prior to this week, it had been anticipated he would be re-elected unopposed. FAs around the world, including some in Europe, have already confirmed their intention to support the 56-year-old.

But sources say in addition to rejecting Infantino's plan, the vast majority of the Concacaf members are either losing faith in the Fifa president's ability to govern the game, or have lost it altogether.

While Uefa members are among the richest on the planet, many nations elsewhere rely on Fifa funding for basic infrastructure.

"There are the aspirations and needs of small nations, but you've also got large nations who have the power," former Football Association chief executive Mark Palios told BBC Breakfast.

"It's not dissimilar to the attempts to form a European Super League. On one end you've got the people who create the cash, but on the other end you still need competition."

Rogers Byamukama of the Ugandan Football Federation argued that any avenue that could lead to more resources for nations like his should be explored.

"First and foremost, you need to understand that football is a very expensive venture, especially on the African continent where the resources are not easy to come by," he told Newsday on BBC World Service.

"For instance in Uganda, the number of infrastructure projects that have been funded by Fifa from the resources generated by Fifa, especially at the World Cup, both from ticket sales as well as sponsors.

"On top of that, there are many grassroot programmes that have been funded by Fifa, including schools for football.

"From my perspective, any avenue that brings in more resources is good because those resources would be distributed and given to federations, especially on the African continent and that would inspire growth."

Byamukama acknowledged Uefa's right to speak out, but suggested that its members are not reliant on Fifa funding like many associations in the rest of the world where Infantino remains popular.

In the first two cycles of the Fifa Forward development programme, through to 2022, $2.8bn (£2.08bn) was made available for investment across the 211 member associations.

Fifa Forward 3.0 - covering the years 2023 through to 2026 - has produced a 30% increase in funding.

Fifa has provided a further $5m (£3.7m) for every member association, with another $60m (£44.48m) paid to each confederation for their own projects.

After being re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023, Infantino is expected to win another term in 2027.

title: Beever-Jones ready to 'conquer' new season after injury troubles last term
description: Chelsea and England forward Aggie Beever-Jones had her "hardest" season in 2025-26 and she had a big decision to make about her future when it ended.
fullText:
England forward Aggie Beever-Jones had her "hardest" season in 2025-26 and when it ended, she had a big decision to make about her future.

Successive ankle injuries meant lengthy periods out of action as Chelsea's title defence faltered, all while her contract was running down.

But despite interest from other Women's Super League clubs, the 23-year-old signed a new four-year deal at Chelsea and intends to play a key role this season as the Blues try to bounce back from a disappointing campaign.

"I look at my career at Chelsea so far and I had quite a successful start," she told BBC Sport.

"Last year, as a club, it was probably our hardest season. We got one trophy, which isn't up to our standards.

"Personally, it was the toughest year with injuries. It put me on the sidelines quite a bit and I really struggled getting consistency back.

"I spent a lot of time this summer recovering to conquer this season and I'm really delighted to have signed a new contract. It definitely felt like the right thing."

Beever-Jones used the summer off to recover and travel, visiting Copenhagen and Los Angeles before grabbing a ticket to watch the men's World Cup final.

In that time, she learned to prioritise her body - something she had not thought about as much previously because of her rapid success and consistent goalscoring form.

Successful loan spells at Bristol City and Everton were followed by 11 goals for Chelsea in the 2023-24 season, finishing with the best minutes-per-goal ratio in the WSL and earning an England call-up.

The season after continued in a similar vein. She was Chelsea's top scorer on the way to an unbeaten domestic treble, and capped by winning Euro 2025 with England.

But last season she learned a harsh lesson, only once completing a full game after Christmas while Manchester City ended Chelsea's six-year stranglehold on the WSL.

"It was extremely tough - it was the first big injury I had," Beever-Jones said of her ankle issues.

"I'm never going to go off the pitch unless I'm in absolute agony. There were a few times where I wanted to carry on pushing and my body was not ready and I really struggled with that.

"The mental side isn't always spoken about enough. My job is to be a footballer and as soon as that's taken away from me, I feel empty.

"It's hard to fill that void. You come to training and you try to put on a brave face but you do feel a little bit isolated.

"There were some dark times but I think that's all part of the journey that you need to go on to really appreciate the good times."

Beever-Jones says she feels "stronger" after that challenging period and is ready to fight for a consistent starting role at Chelsea.

She also has her mind on the Women's World Cup next year and to catch England manager Sarina Wiegman's eye as the Lionesses attempt to reach a fourth successive major final.

The striker has netted seven goals in 16 England appearances, including a memorable first-half hat-trick against Portugal at Wembley in 2025.

However, she has often found herself below Alessia Russo and, at Euro 2025, Michelle Agyemang in the pecking order - so is this a crucial season for Beever-Jones?

"That's why I was so gaffed about last year," she said. "[The World Cup is] my ambition and I hope I can get there, but I've just got to take each day as it comes."

Beever-Jones reminded WSL fans of her abilities with a starring role at the World Sevens in May where she scored six goals, including Chelsea's winner in the final against Manchester United.

"The World Sevens tournament was such a good time for me. It was finally when I felt back at full fitness and I was ready to go," she added.

"It was a shame that the season came to an end then but that was me in my flow state - when I'm happy, I'm enjoying it and I'm not playing in pain.

"Obviously it's a really big year with the World Cup and I just hope I can help to grow the game and Chelsea can dominate domestically and in Europe."

Clubs lower down the WSL such as London City Lionesses, Tottenham and Brighton have all made big investments in their playing squads this summer.

At the top end, champions Manchester City have added England internationals Beth Mead and Niamh Charles - from Chelsea - while Arsenal have also strengthened.

However, prior to last season's disappointment, Chelsea had won six successive WSL titles, while they have been in every Women's League Cup final since 2019 and have reached the semi-finals of the Women's Champions League in three of the past four campaigns.

So is it foolish to write them off this season?

"There's been a lot of noise around Chelsea. Other teams are signing but you look at our squad and I'd still say we have incredible, world-class players," said Beever-Jones.

"We've brought in Katie McCabe, Melvine Malard, Manaka Matsukubo - world-class players who have already really impressed.

"We're doing the work behind the scenes that doesn't always get put out in the media. I'm confident within the team we share that common goal.

"I believe we'll show that when we need to. I have every faith that it will be us that wins and that we'll work hard."

fullText:
Hidden gems can be unearthed, but you have to dig deep into the bargain bins of countless outdated Fifas, Wii Fits without the controllers and partially finished quizshow games

As an eternally optimistic charity shop fan, I hold on to the fantasy that one day I’ll walk into my local Oxfam and find a pristine copy of the Sega Saturn shooter Burning Rangers for £1.50. Or perhaps a box full of old Neo Geo carts for a quid each. Sadly, this is now unlikely. Charity shops have caught on to the fact that old video games – like old vinyl albums – are highly collectible, and so they’re putting the good stuff on eBay. That’s fine, it’s their job to raise money, not to provide opportunist swine like me with bargains. But what games can you find tucked away in your local branch of Barnardo’s? To find out I visited about 40 charity stores across the country. Here is what I discovered on the shelves … And please do share your own charity shop gaming finds in the comments!

Titles such as Dr Kawashima’s Brain Training and Big Brain Academy sold in their millions on the DS and Wii in the mid-00s, accelerated by smart, celebrity-crammed TV advertising. Naturally, there were reams of imitators – seemingly all of which have ended up on charity shop shelves. The original Brain Training is still challenging and fun – although if you grab a copy, be careful to check any saved game files still left in the cart’s memory. I got a copy for a quid, and when I loaded it up, one of the stored usernames was “Martin’s Sex Bitch” (brain age: 35). Steer well clear of all the TV quiz show games that clogged up the DS library. One charity shop I went into had just a single game: Golden Balls, based on the daytime gameshow presented by Jasper Carrott. Reader: I did not buy it.

This was another ubiquitous category. No matter where I went, charity shops were filled with copies of Dance UK, SingStar and Wii Fit, but all lacked the necessary controllers to make them work. There were Kinect games with no Kinect and PlayStation EyeToy games with no camera. Out of all of them, I’d be tempted most by PlayStation 2 SingStar titles – it’ll only cost about £12 on eBay to buy the microphones and adaptor, then you can pick up the dozens of SingStar instalments for a few pounds (Rock Ballads! Motown! Sing along with Disney!) – hey presto, karaoke heaven. Wii Fit is also OK if you’re happy to pay £10 for a balance board on eBay that hasn’t been pounded to death.

Once again, these proliferated on the family-friendly Wii and DS consoles and as they hold little replay value, they show up in great numbers. Peppa Pig, Pirates of the Caribbean, lots of pet games – one store I found in Brighton had at least five horse sims, including Horse Life and Pippa Funnell. Ubisoft’s range of job sims including Imagine: Fashion Designer and Imagine: Teacher were in abundance, though sadly, I didn’t find a copy of Imagine: Journalist, which would have been useful. One title in this genre that was present in at least 65% of the shops I visited was Carnival Games from 2K Play, a wretched collection of fairground mini-challenges including duck shoot, ring toss and balloon darts. The motion controls are appalling and the player avatars are terrifying, dead-eyed monstrosities. If the backrooms had a games area, this would be playing.

Some games sold so well, they have absolutely no value in the secondhand market. You can always count on finding a number of Call of Duty, Assassin’s Creed or Gears of War instalments as well as many copies of GTA V. Some of these are worth rediscovering. The campaign modes in Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare, Modern Warfare 2 and Infinite Warfare are fun, while Assassin’s Creed Brotherhood, Origins and Odyssey are all worth playing – as is Assassin’s Creed 2. I’d also buy Gears of War 2 and Halo 2 for the campaign modes if you’ve not played them. The Mass Effect and Dragon Age titles are often knocking about and still have a lot of charm.

These are still clogging the shelves of charity shops everywhere, despite (or perhaps because of) the fact that a lot of PC owners no longer have CD-Rom drives, and even if they did, they’re likely to face compatibility issues trying to load ancient copies of, say, The Sims 2 or saucy adult adventure title, Leisure Suit Larry: Box Office Bust (the latter might still be in the Frome branch of the Cats and Dogs charity shop if you’re interested). With digital stores such as Steam and GOG stuffed with retro titles at teeny prices, there’s little reason to buy disc PC games now – unless you stumble across an ancient “big box” copy of Doom, Half-Life or Zak McKracken and the Alien Mindbenders. Which you won’t.

They’re still out there, especially at pop-up charity shops and smaller independent stores. I bagged a copy of the rare Japanese role-playing adventure Koudelka at the Rotary Club shop in Frome for a pound, and feel a little guilty about it. I also recently acquired the light gun titles Time Crisis II (PS2) and Time Crisis: Razing Storm (PS3) for £3 each – and I even have a G-Con 2 and PlayStation Move controller to play them with. Elsewhere, I’ve regularly spotted copies of Dead Rising, Bulletstorm, FEAR and Project Gotham Racing – all great fun. Oh and fellow games contributor Jordan Erica Webber recently found Tiger Electronics’ handheld LCD game Poke Ball at the Cats Protection shop in Leamington Spa. I’d have snapped that up.

But if you do find a copy of Burning Rangers on the Sega Saturn it is completely worthless and terrible and you should just send it straight to me.

fullText:
Company says it discovered unauthorized access during ‘proactive review’ after rival OpenAI revealed rogue agent

Anthropic ⁠said on Thursday its AI Claude model hacked ⁠systems of ⁠three ​organizations during testing, days after rival OpenAI ⁠revealed a rogue agent had gone on a days-long ⁠hacking spree at AI ​firm Hugging ‌Face.

Claude gained ‌unauthorized access to the ‌systems during cybersecurity evaluations after a misconfiguration allowed the models to reach the internet from testing environments that ‌were supposed to be isolated, Anthropic said.

The company said ​it identified the incidents after reviewing 141,006 cybersecurity evaluation runs, a process it ⁠launched following OpenAI’s disclosures.

The ‌breaches signal that AI’s expanding capabilities are already fueling the security threat experts have long feared ‌and that even top developers can be caught off-guard by flaws their models can exploit.

“Claude compromised the ​impacted ​organizations’ infrastructure using ​basic techniques, such as ​exploiting ‌weak passwords and ​unauthenticated ​endpoints,” it said.

Anthropic said the incidents involved three separate models: Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Mythos 5 and an internal research model. The earliest cases dated back to April and ‌occurred in evaluation environments that lacked what the company described as standard safeguards.

The breaches occurred during the so-called “capture the flag” exercises, in which models were tasked with finding ​hidden information in simulated networks. The company said its prompts told the models they had no internet access, but a misunderstanding with its evaluation partner Irregular left the systems connected to the public internet.

Two of the organizations were ​unaware of the activity ‌before being contacted, Anthropic ​said, adding that ​it was still trying to reach the third.

“We discovered these incidents after a proactive review of our cybersecurity evaluation transcripts,” the company said in a statement.

The findings underscore the need for stronger controls in both internal and third-party testing environments as AI models become increasingly capable of carrying out real-world cyber activities, Anthropic said.

Sainsbury’s boss Simon Roberts decided to about turn when he took over in 2020, focusing on food, which has much higher barriers to entry for Amazon or other Chinese players because of the cold chain logistics required to keep food fresh.

The buyer will be Swift Partners, new company established for the deal by former Co-operative supermarket chief executive Richard Pennycook, former Morrisons executive Trevor Strain and banker Matt Truman.

What attracted us to Argos is the strength of the business, with a trusted brand, loyal customers and dedicated colleagues. We believe strongly in Argos’s future and see real opportunities to invest and build on its progress.

Argos’s combination - of a strong digital business supported by standalone stores, stores inside Sainsbury’s and local fulfilment centres - gives it a distinctive position in the market and an excellent platform for growth.

fullText:
Across the country, workers are fearful about the impact of AI on their livelihoods in an increasingly fragile labour market

On the tree-lined streets of Wuhan, where cars jostle for space with mopeds and cargo trucks, the malfunctioning of a new type of vehicle has recently been causing chaos on the city’s roads.

In March, several cars from a fleet of driverless taxis stopped abruptly in the streets. The “system malfunction” left distressed riders stranded for hours. The robotaxis, known as Apollo Go and powered by artificial intelligence (AI), were taken off Wuhan’s streets for months for investigations.

But the outage was a boon for 45-year-old taxi driver Yao Xinnong. His wages, which had fallen by about 40% since Apollo Go launched in 2022, jumped back up as customers returned.

“I don’t really like them, to be honest,” Yao says of the driverless cabs operated by the tech giant Baidu. “Their impact has been huge”.

China is encouraging the deployment of AI at a scale unseen in the west. The technology is being rolled out at a staggering rate in an increasingly precarious labour market, and the Wuhan episode helped to highlight the social tensions it is causing.

Gig workers like Yao are fearful about the impact of AI on their livelihoods, while recent incidents of white-collar workers being replaced by AI have also sparked a debate over whether workers should embrace the technology – or try to compete with it.

Addressing Shanghai’s World AI Conference in July, China’s leader, Xi Jinping, said that AI should be “an important driver for shared prosperity and common security”.

But that goal is being pursued amid an increasingly fragile labour market. As well as suffering from high levels of unemployment, China has seen tens of millions of workers drop out of formal employment into the gig economy. According to one thinktank, the number of people in flexible employment will rise to 320 million this year, up from 160 million in 2019. That is about 44% of China’s workforce.

Taxi drivers are one part of this huge cohort. Across the country, as previously heavyweight industries such as real estate and education have floundered, workers have turned to ride-hailing apps to make ends meet. But now the rollout of robotaxis, one of the most popular applications of AI that is already in use in China, is threatening their livelihoods.

“If the state really took you into consideration, Apollo Go would never have gone on the market,” says one Wuhan driver.

“If things keep going this way in the future, sure, rapid development and scientific progress are great, but ordinary people like us will have no place to survive,” she adds.

In 2024, taxi drivers in Wuhan protested against the rollout of Apollo Go in their city. It is unclear how many people took part, because news of the protests were quickly censored. Several drivers interviewed in Wuhan said they had heard about the protests but denied being involved.

That year, a Wuhan taxi company, took the rare step of publicly criticising the government’s policy to allow automation on to the city’s streets.

“The recent rise of autonomous ride-hailing vehicles has allowed technology to monopolise resources and take away the livelihoods of people at the bottom of society,” the letter said.

Authorities in China do not take kindly to public criticism. When the Guardian visited the taxi company’s office in July, an employee declined to be interviewed, citing an agreement with the police to refuse interviews and the risk of detention if he violated the agreement.

But two years later, the government is echoing some of the same concerns first voiced by the Wuhan drivers.

An editorial published in the state-run Workers’ Daily said that employment rights were “facing new challenges” in the age of AI. The article warned of a “collision between traditional employment rules and the iteration of AI technology”.

The government recently pledged to “comprehensively address the impact of changes in the external environment and the development of new technologies such as artificial intelligence on employment”.

Selina Xu, a China technology analyst, said there had been a “major vibe shift” from Beijing.

She says that after the success of local AI model DeepSeek last year, China was “very pro AI development”.

“This year, if you look at certain new guidelines that have been published … there has been a lot more emphasis placed on AI for boosting employment and people-first approaches,” Xu says.

Cheng Wanhui, an official for the local government in Beijing’s hi-tech zone of Zhongguancun, says that the authorities are “paying close attention to the social issues AI brings, as well as potential ethical concerns.”

“The key is for everyone to shift their mindset, see AI as a tool, and learn how to apply it in their future work,” Cheng says.

Recent court rulings have awarded compensation to white-collar workers laid off by their firms to be replaced by AI. But many workers fear the AI uptake will be a barrier to them being offered a job in the first place.

Tian Zemin, a cinematographer who works in Beijing, has worked in the film industry for nearly two decades. But now he’s out of work. “I spent six gruelling years working my way up to become a cinematographer, only to be replaced by a piece of software,” he wrote in a social media post about AI.

“I thought I would spend my whole life in this industry. But the emergence of AI has made me feel a huge shock for the first time,” he tells the Guardian.

Many of Tian’s peers are losing out as AI becomes more widely adopted across the film industry. His own rate as a freelancer is now 40% of what it was in 2019.

Tian said he’s been shocked at AI’s progress. Last year, it made shonky, weird looking avatars. Now it can make convincing digital clones who have the range to carry a feature length film. “We have barely had time to react,” Tian says.

Many analysts believe that China, where the government exerts significant control over the private sector, will be better placed than the US to contain the fallout from AI-related job losses. Beijing could for example instruct companies to comply with hiring quotas, Xu says.

But for Tian, protections may not come soon enough. “We could be replaced at any moment,” he says. “Perhaps the only thing we can do is adapt as quickly as possible, and try to find the corner that AI still cannot replace – but that corner is getting smaller and smaller.”

How injury changed Ditcheva's outlook on life beyond MMA
description: Dakota Ditcheva returns to the cage after a year away with two serious hand injuries, but says her time on the sidelines has changed her outlook on fighting, the UFC and life after MMA.
fullText:
When Dakota Ditcheva makes her PFL return against Denise Kielholtz in New York City on Friday night, she will do so with a very different mindset.

It has been a year like no other for Ditcheva, who has been sidelined by injury since breaking her left hand against Sumiko Inaba in July 2025.

The British-Bulgarian, unbeaten in her 15-fight professional career, was scheduled to return against Keilholtz in February, but the fight was postponed after she suffered another significant injury, this time to her right hand.

For Ditcheva, who won the PFL flyweight tournament and $1m (£740,000) in 2024, her time away has underlined the importance of building a successful career outside the cage.

"It has been tough, and I have been really lucky that I am building things outside of the sport where I have other things I can do and keep busy," Ditcheva told BBC Sport.

"That has always been a really big thing for me. I always say that when I am done being a fighter, I want to be set up in other things because these moments, where things are taken away from you, kind of give you an insight into what life is going to be like when you stop fighting. Like, 'now what?"'

It is something her mother, Lisa Howarth, understands only too well. A former kickboxing and Muay Thai world champion, Howarth successfully built a career in the police after retiring from combat sports.

"She has always said right from the beginning that you need to set something up because she didn't really do that," Ditcheva said.

"She had an amazing career afterwards because of the type of person she is, but she didn't set anything up that she could have got from the sport."

In January 2025, Ditcheva, 28, took her first steps into the world of business by co-founding a premium mineral water brand.

"Back in England, you get a pension after you've finished some jobs, so you're set up for later in life. Fighters don't get that," Ditcheva said.

"Our promotions don't take a cut of our money to save for after we've retired."

While some fighters struggle financially, with pay continuing to be a topic of debate, others find it difficult to replace the routine of a training camp and the sense of purpose provided by having a fight date to work towards.

In June, ex-UFC fighter Dustin Poirier, who trained with Ditcheva at American Top Team, said he was "at the point where I need some help" after being arrested for alleged public drunkenness.

Ditcheva says she has not spoken directly with Poirier but, having spent 12 months on the sidelines, recognises how the absence of training and fighting can take a toll.

"It is sad to see a lot of people online saying what they are saying because he [Poirier] is just a normal guy who is struggling with a feeling that not one person outside of the sport will understand," Ditcheva said.

"Unless you can feel the adrenaline rush we get, and understand that it's a feeling you can't get from anything else, you won't understand what he is going through after giving up fighting.

"I think he's doing the right thing, from what I have seen online, and focusing on himself. That's the best thing he can do."

Ditcheva has been a dominant force in the organisation, winning all 10 of her fights and securing seven of those victories in the opening round.

That has led to suggestions that a move to the UFC could be on the horizon, though Ditcheva told BBC Sport she still has five fights remaining on her contract.

But earlier this month, Ditcheva's manager said her current PFL deal would make her one of the highest-paid female fighters in the UFC.

"I'm enjoying my career. I'm living a good life. I'm changing my family's life here at the PFL, and I feel like it is suiting me right now," Ditcheva said.

"Will I go over to the UFC one day? I don't know. Maybe that's not in my plan any more. Maybe I'll box. I don't know."

On Thursday, the PFL announced it had agreed to merge with Jake Paul's Most Valuable Promotions - making staying put an even more attractive prospect.

That opens the door to potentially moving into the sphere of boxing and could also produce opportunities of super-fights in MMA.

"You see every fighter say they want to go to the UFC, and that used to be me," Ditcheva said.

"I don't know whether it is any more. I feel like my goals are changing all the time, and the opportunities I'm getting I'm really enjoying.

"Is the UFC the be-all and end-all? I don't know any more.

"It's not something that will ever define me. If I end my career and I have never been to the UFC, nobody is going to make me feel bad online about it.

"If I end my career having been undefeated, I'm still undefeated and the number one flyweight whether I go to the UFC or not."

title: De Zerbi's 'ultra' roots and the Brescia connection at Spurs
description: Roberto de Zerbi says he was born an ultra, raised on the Brescia curva alongside his father - and he has carried those roots to north London.
fullText:
There is a distinctly Brescian feel to N17 of late. While the Italian city's famous old club were effectively declared bankrupt this week, a footballing passion forged at Stadio Mario Rigamonti may be fuelling Tottenham Hotspur's revival.

Roberto de Zerbi, the manager who saved Spurs from relegation last season, was raised on the terraces of Brescia's 'curva' by his father, Alfredo, who was president of the supporters' clubs. De Zerbi says he was "born an ultra".

"My dad is crazy about football. He was one of the leaders of the Brescia tifoseria. At home, we lived and breathed football. He was the one who passed that passion on to me," the Italian told Salim Lamrani in his book Football According to Roberto de Zerbi.

Tottenham's Brescia connection runs through the playing squad too. Sandro Tonali, their new record signing, joined Le Rondinelle aged 12 and made his debut as a 17-year-old, helping Brescia return to Serie A before joining AC Milan in 2020.

De Zerbi says he followed the midfielder as he rose through the ranks at his boyhood club, and Tonali told BBC Sport on Thursday about the bond they share.

"Brescia is so small. I had two weeks there and met him two or three times," he said.

"We spoke about Brescia, about the difficult situation facing our club."

However, Tonali's £100m move threatened to pose a contentious issue in Italy.

Amid mounting debt and financial problems, Brescia Calcio, owned by Massimo Cellino, were excluded from professional football by Italian authorities last summer.

They were replaced by a new team in Union Brescia, who have taken on the mantle of the city's club and play at the same iconic ground graced by Roberto Baggio and Pep Guardiola, as well as De Zerbi and Tonali.

Tonali and his wife were there to watch Union Brescia in the Serie C play-offs earlier this year - the club eventually lost to Ascoli in the final.

There were reports, however, that Cellino may look to revive Brescia Calcio in some format with the club, having trained Tonali, potentially due a percentage of his transfer fee - about £3.5m - under Fifa's solidarity contribution scheme.

But that prospect seems to have died after Brescia Calcio were wound-up in a court ruling, external on Tuesday.

As Brescia and their fans embrace a new era, the passion and footballing ethos De Zerbi learned through his father and those visits to Stadio Mario Rigamonti remain.

"Roberto's love for Brescia shaped his career," his brother, Rocco, told Corriere Della Sera.

Tonali 'took 10 minutes' to decide to join Spurs

The downfall of Brescia & rebirth in Serie C

Rosanna Pedrollo spent half a century working for Brescia, first joining the club's administration department in 1968 - she met De Zerbi's father, Alfredo, in the early 1980s through his work coordinating the supporters' clubs.

"He was always around in those days," Pedrollo tells BBC Sport. "He organised the away trips, knew which players were going to visit which supporters' clubs and when. He took care of everything.

"Alfredo was a huge football fan. He was a passionate, fiery character and a wonderful father. He was a gentle person, but full of energy at the same time. Very polite, but never afraid to say what he thought, whether people agreed with him or not.

"There aren't many people like him in football today. Everything has changed so much. He gave his passion to the club."

Pedrollo remembers a four or five-year-old De Zerbi being mascot, when he would follow the side home and away with his father. 'Roby', as his friends called him, would also watch training sessions and prepare tifos for home matches.

He happened to be a talented footballer, too, playing a stone's throw from his idols for USO Mompiano, before joining lower-league side Lumezzane and then AC Milan at the age of 12.

His father "wanted so badly" to see him play for Brescia one day, says Pedrollo, adding: "That I know for certain, because he told me many times."

Alfredo got his wish when his son spent 19 games on loan at his hometown club in 2008.

De Zerbi got his first taste for coaching in the city too, helping a friend coach youngsters at ADC Mario Rigamonti, yet many of the principles that guide his management today took root through the adversity his family faced in the economic crisis of the early '90s.

His father was forced to sell their mat factory, as well as the home De Zerbi grew up in, instead moving into a small flat.

"We had to rebuild our lives from scratch," De Zerbi told Lamrani, who says the Italian remains "true to the ideals of his youth and to his working-class roots".

Indeed, the day after signing his first professional contract with Milan, De Zerbi says he was at the bank signing a mortgage to buy his parents a house.

"Coming from a modest background, success has never led him to abandon his principles or his values," adds Lamrani, who also worked as Marcelo Bielsa's disciplinary coach and interpreter at Leeds United.

"He has preserved the principles of solidarity and generosity instilled in him by his parents and has never renounced his social origins. He knows exactly which side of the barricades he stands on: with the people.

"He instinctively sides with the oppressed. That reflects his rebellious temperament, forged by his own life story."

Lamrani says De Zerbi "remains deeply attached to the people on the terraces" - and to his Brescian roots. That was obvious when Marseille welcomed Atalanta in the Champions League last season.

George Boxall, author of FADA! A Season in Marseille, who followed De Zerbi's time in France, recalls the Italian performing the famous Brescia 'V' sign towards the away end.

"I was born in Brescia, a hundred metres from the stadium; I'm a Brescia tifoso - it's in my family's DNA - and for us, playing Atalanta is like a fiercely contested derby; we'd be thinking about it from Monday to Sunday," said De Zerbi at the time.

"Roberto is a man of the terraces, a man of the people: straightforward, loyal and authentic," adds Lamrani.

"He loves terrace culture, particularly at working-class clubs such as OM. He grew up on the streets and absorbed their unwritten codes. For him, a person's word is sacred.

"He is generous by nature, giving of himself without reserve and trusting his instincts. He has little patience for selfishness or opportunism. That outlook is deeply rooted in ultra culture."
